sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Core Identity**: The 'Chuars' were local tribal cultivators and 'Paiks' (traditional village police) in the **Jungle Mahals** (Bankura, Midnapore, Manbhum). 
• **Primary Trigger**: The imposition of the **Permanent Settlement (1793)** which replaced traditional tribal land rights with a rigid, exploitative revenue system. 
• **Economic Displacement**: The resumption of **Paikan lands** (rent-free lands held by Paiks) by the British to maximize revenue, leading to the loss of livelihood for the tribal militia. 
• **Key Metric / Factor**: The uprising was not a single event but a protracted struggle spanning five decades, characterized by guerrilla warfare and the burning of British administrative outposts.

items.definition: Land grants given to the Paiks (village guards) in lieu of salary. Resumption of these lands by the British was the primary catalyst for the revolt.
An administrative district created by the British in 1805 to manage the volatile tribal regions of Bengal and Bihar.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Guerrilla Tactics**: Use of dense forest terrain to ambush British forces.
• **Coalition Building**: Alliance between displaced tribal Zamindars and the common peasantry against the new 'outsider' landlords (Dikus).

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Lack of centralized leadership and modern weaponry compared to the British military.
• **Solutions**: The movement forced the British to eventually create the 'Jungle Mahals' district, acknowledging the need for a distinct administrative approach for tribal areas.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'JDM' (Jagannath, Durjan, Madhab) - The leaders of the Chuar Uprising.
• **Decoded Meaning**: J (Jagannath Singh), D (Durjan Singh), M (Madhab Singh). Remember: 'Chuars were JDM-driven'.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the Chuar Uprising with the Santhal Rebellion. Remember: Chuar is 18th-19th century (1766-1816), while Santhal is mid-19th century (1855-56).
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Subaltern Resistance' to describe the Chuar Uprising, highlighting the agency of tribal groups against colonial structural violence.

keyTakeaways: The Chuar Uprising was a reaction to the disruption of the traditional Paikan land tenure system.
It was a precursor to later tribal movements, highlighting the failure of early colonial land revenue policies.
The movement was geographically concentrated in the Jungle Mahals and led by displaced tribal chieftains.
